title: Why UX Research Is the Foundation of Every Great Design
excerpt: Before jumping into wireframes or Figma, the real work starts with understanding the people who will actually use your product.
content:
Every project I work on starts with questions.

Who is this product for? What problem are we actually trying to solve? What does the user currently do when this product doesn't exist?

It's tempting to jump directly into Figma. Designers love designing, after all. Opening a blank canvas and immediately exploring layouts feels productive. But a beautiful interface built on assumptions can still become a terrible product.

That's where UX research comes in.

Designing Without Research Means Designing Around Assumptions

Every project begins with assumptions. Sometimes they come from the client, sometimes from stakeholders and sometimes from the designer.

The problem isn't having assumptions. The problem is treating them as facts.

A feature that seems obvious to the team might be completely irrelevant to the people actually using the product. A navigation structure that makes sense internally might confuse a first-time visitor. Even something as simple as a button label can create friction when it doesn't match the language users naturally use.

Research helps us replace some of those assumptions with evidence.

Research Doesn't Always Need to Be Complicated

When people hear the term UX research, they sometimes imagine expensive studies, massive surveys and months of analysis.

Research can be much simpler than that.

Depending on the project, it might involve interviewing a few potential users, reviewing customer feedback, analyzing competitors, studying existing analytics or simply observing how people currently complete a task.

The goal isn't to collect as much information as possible. The goal is to learn enough to make better decisions.

Research Changes the Questions You Ask

Without research, designers often ask: What should we build?

After talking to users, the question often becomes: Do we actually need to build this?

That difference can save an enormous amount of time.

I've seen projects where an initial idea involved adding more features, more options and more information to an interface. After looking at the actual user journey, the real opportunity was the opposite: remove unnecessary steps and make the most important action easier to find.

Sometimes the best design decision isn't adding something new. It's recognizing what can be removed.

Good Research Creates Shared Understanding

One of the biggest benefits of research isn't even the final report.

It's alignment.

When designers, developers and stakeholders have a shared understanding of the user's problems, conversations become much more productive. Decisions stop being based entirely on personal preference.

Instead of saying, 'I think users would prefer this,' the conversation can become, 'Here's what we learned from users. How can we solve this problem?'

The Design Comes After

Research doesn't remove creativity from the design process. It gives creativity direction.

Once you understand the problem, you have something meaningful to design around.

That's why I don't see research as a phase that happens before design. It's part of design.

A great interface isn't simply one that looks polished. It's one that understands the person sitting on the other side of the screen.

title: Good UI Isn't About Making Everything Look Pretty
excerpt: A visually impressive interface can still be frustrating to use. Good UI has to do more than look good.
content:
One of the biggest misconceptions about UI design is that the goal is simply to make things look good.

Of course, aesthetics matter. A polished interface can build trust, communicate personality and make a product feel more enjoyable to use.

But appearance alone isn't enough.

An interface can have beautiful gradients, smooth animations and perfect typography while still making users wonder where they need to click next.

Visual Design Should Support the Experience

Every visual decision should have a purpose.

Typography creates hierarchy. Color helps users understand relationships and actions. Spacing separates information. Contrast guides attention.

When these elements work together, users don't have to consciously analyze the interface. They simply move through it.

Less Visual Noise, More Clarity

Sometimes the strongest UI decision is removing something.

Not every section needs an illustration. Not every button needs a gradient. Not every piece of information deserves the same visual importance.

Design is communication, and communication becomes difficult when everything is shouting at the same time.

Before adding another visual element, I like to ask a simple question: Does this help the user understand something, or does it just make the screen busier?

The Real Test

A good-looking interface might get someone's attention.

A good interface helps them accomplish what they came to do.

The best UI usually manages to do both.

title: The Best User Experience Is Often Invisible
excerpt: When everything works exactly as expected, users rarely stop to admire the experience. And honestly, that's usually a good sign.
content:
Think about the last time you used an app and everything worked perfectly.

You probably didn't close it and think, 'Wow, that was an incredible user experience.'

You simply accomplished what you needed to do and moved on.

That's one of the strange things about UX. When it works well, it often becomes invisible.

Users notice friction. They notice confusing navigation, unclear buttons and forms that ask for unnecessary information.

But when an experience feels natural, most people don't stop to think about the design behind it.

And that's okay.

Our job isn't always to make users notice the interface. Sometimes it's to make sure the interface doesn't get in their way.

title: Why White Space Is Not Empty Space
excerpt: If a screen feels too empty, the instinct is often to add more. In many cases, that's exactly what makes the design worse.
content:
I've seen this happen in design reviews many times: someone looks at a layout and says, 'There is too much empty space.'

The instinct is understandable. An empty area can feel like unused space that needs to be filled.

But white space isn't wasted space.

It's one of the tools that allows information to breathe.

Space Creates Relationships

The distance between elements communicates something.

Items placed close together are usually perceived as related. Elements separated by larger gaps feel like different groups.

This means spacing isn't just decoration. It's part of the information architecture of a screen.

More Content Doesn't Always Mean More Value

When every area of an interface is filled with cards, buttons, images and text, users have to work harder to understand what matters.

Giving important elements room to breathe can actually make them easier to notice.

White Space Creates Focus

A good layout doesn't try to make users look at everything.

It helps them understand what deserves their attention first.

So the next time a design feels 'too empty,' I think the better question is not how can we fill this space?

It's whether the space is helping the content around it work better.

title: Design Trends Are Inspiration, Not Instructions
excerpt: Following every new visual trend might make a design feel current, but it won't necessarily make it better.
content:
Design trends are fun. I enjoy exploring them just as much as anyone else.

New visual styles can introduce fresh ideas, challenge familiar patterns and push the industry in interesting directions.

The problem starts when we treat a trend as a requirement.

A Trend Doesn't Know Your User

A visual trend doesn't understand your audience, your product or the problem you're trying to solve.

Just because a particular style looks great in a design gallery doesn't automatically mean it belongs in a banking app, an educational platform or a business dashboard.

Context matters.

Ask Why Before You Copy

Before using a new visual style, I think it's worth asking why it works.

Does the approach improve hierarchy? Does it make the experience more engaging? Does it fit the personality of the product?

If the only answer is 'because everyone is doing it,' that's probably not enough.

Good Design Has a Longer Lifespan

Trends change quickly. Principles like clarity, accessibility and usability tend to stay relevant.

That doesn't mean avoiding trends completely. It means using them intentionally.

The best designers don't simply follow what's popular. They understand when a new idea is actually useful.

title: Your Users Don't Care How Much Work You Put Into the Interface
excerpt: You might have spent hours perfecting an interaction. The user only cares whether it helps them get something done.
content:
Designers can become emotionally attached to their work.

We've all spent hours adjusting spacing, refining a component or building a beautiful interaction that we're particularly proud of.

But here's the uncomfortable truth: users don't care how long it took you.

They care about whether the product works.

They don't know how many iterations your dashboard required. They don't know how complicated the prototype was.

And honestly, they shouldn't have to.

A user's experience shouldn't become more difficult just because the team invested a lot of time building a particular feature.

Good design sometimes requires letting go of something you like because it doesn't actually help the user.

That's difficult. But it's part of the job.

title: Accessibility Shouldn't Be a Final Checklist
excerpt: Accessibility isn't something we should remember right before launching a product. It should influence decisions from the beginning.
content:
Accessibility is often treated as something that happens at the end of a project.

The product is almost finished, the screens look polished and then someone asks: 'Is it accessible?'

At that point, teams often discover problems that would have been much easier to solve earlier.

Accessibility works better when it becomes part of the design process from the beginning.

Accessibility Is About People, Not Just Requirements

It's easy to think about accessibility as a list of technical requirements.

Contrast ratios. Keyboard navigation. Alternative text.

Those things matter, but the real purpose is much larger: making sure more people can successfully use the product.

A color combination that looks beautiful might be impossible to distinguish for someone with low vision. A complex interaction might be difficult to complete without a mouse. A form that relies entirely on color to communicate an error can leave some users without the information they need.

These aren't edge cases. They're real experiences.

Accessible Design Often Improves the Product for Everyone

One of my favorite things about accessibility is that many accessible decisions benefit more people than we initially expect.

Clear labels help everyone. Better contrast can make an interface easier to use outdoors. Captions help people watching videos in noisy environments. Large interactive areas make mobile interfaces easier to use.

Designing for a wider range of needs often leads to a stronger experience overall.

Start Earlier

Instead of asking whether a finished design is accessible, we should ask accessibility-related questions while designing.

Can this information be understood without relying only on color? What happens when someone navigates with a keyboard? Is the hierarchy still clear when someone changes their text size?

These questions are easier to answer before development begins.

Accessibility Is Part of Good Design

I don't see accessibility as a separate feature that gets added to a product.

It's part of the definition of a good product.

If a user can't understand, navigate or interact with your interface, it doesn't matter how visually impressive it looks.

A design isn't truly complete if some of the people it's supposed to serve were never considered in the first place.

title: Why Every Designer Should Learn Basic Frontend
excerpt: You don't need to become a full-stack developer, but understanding how your designs are built can completely change the way you design.
content:
I don't think every UI/UX designer needs to become a developer.

But I do think understanding the basics of frontend development can make you a better designer.

Designing Becomes More Realistic

When you understand how HTML, CSS and responsive layouts work, you start making decisions differently.

You begin thinking about what happens when text becomes longer. You consider different screen sizes. You understand that a component isn't just a static frame inside Figma.

It has states, behavior and technical limitations.

Better Conversations With Developers

One of the biggest advantages is communication.

You don't need to know how to write production-level code to have a useful conversation with developers.

Understanding concepts like CSS layouts, reusable components and responsive behavior allows you to explain your design decisions more clearly.

Design Is Not Isolated From Development

At the end of the day, most digital products need to be built.

Understanding that process doesn't limit creativity. It helps you design solutions that can actually exist outside the design tool.

You don't need to become an expert developer.

But learning a little code can give you a completely different perspective on your own work.

title: A Design System Is More Than a Collection of Components
excerpt: A library full of buttons and cards is useful, but a real design system is about consistency, decisions and collaboration.
content:
One of the most common mistakes when talking about design systems is confusing them with UI kits.

A UI kit gives you components.

A design system gives those components context.

Components Are Only the Beginning

Buttons, inputs, cards and navigation elements are important. They help teams build interfaces faster and maintain visual consistency.

But simply placing a collection of components inside a Figma file doesn't automatically create a design system.

A useful system should also answer questions.

When should this component be used? Which variation should we choose? What happens when the component is disabled or loading? How does it behave on smaller screens?

Consistency Is About More Than Visual Style

Consistency isn't simply using the same blue button everywhere.

It's also about creating predictable interactions.

If a user learns how something works in one section of a product, they should ideally be able to use that knowledge somewhere else.

That reduces the amount of learning required to navigate the interface.

A System Should Help Teams Work Together

The strongest design systems aren't created only for designers.

They become a shared language between design and development.

When both teams understand the purpose and behavior of components, fewer decisions need to be reinvented for every new screen.

Documentation Matters

Without documentation, even the best component library eventually becomes difficult to maintain.

People need to understand not only what exists, but why it exists and how it should be used.

A design system isn't a finished project that you create once and forget.

Products evolve. Teams change. New problems appear.

The system should evolve with them.

title: AI Can Help Designers, But It Can't Replace Understanding
excerpt: AI can generate ideas, interfaces and content in seconds. Understanding whether those solutions actually make sense is still a different skill.
content:
AI is changing the way designers work.

It can help us brainstorm, summarize information, generate early concepts and speed up repetitive tasks.

That's useful.

But generating something is not the same as understanding whether it solves the right problem.

An AI tool can produce a beautiful dashboard in seconds. It doesn't automatically know which information is most important to your specific users or what frustrates them during their daily workflow.

That's where designers still matter.

Our value isn't limited to moving pixels around a screen. It's in asking questions, understanding context and making decisions when there isn't an obvious answer.

I don't think AI will eliminate good designers.

I think it will make the ability to think critically even more important.
